subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Cervical cancer is a malignant tumor of the cervix, usually driven by persistent high‑risk HPV infection. Early detection by screening allows curative treatment; advanced disease spreads locally and distally.

sections.p: A malignant neoplasm arising from the squamous epithelium or glandular cells of the cervix. Diagnosis requires histologic confirmation from a biopsy of a suspicious lesion.
b: Histology (squamous cell carcinoma ~70%, adenocarcinoma ~25%)
Screening: HPV DNA testing and visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) in low‑resource settings

t.b: Confirms presence and type of cancer; positive result establishes diagnosis, negative result may need repeat or excisional procedure
Detects high‑risk HPV (16/18); a positive test in a woman >30 prompts colposcopy, a negative test lowers immediate cancer risk

sections.p: Staging follows the FIGO system, based on clinical exam and imaging when available.
b: Stage I: confined to cervix
Stage II: beyond uterus, not to pelvic wall or lower third of vagina
Stage III: lower third vagina or pelvic wall, or hydronephrosis
Stage IV: distant metastasis

t.b: Determines tumor size and parametrial involvement; helps assign FIGO stage
Assesses hydronephrosis or distant spread; absence of imaging defaults to clinical staging

sections.p: Persistent infection with high‑risk HPV types 16 and 18 is the primary cause. Co‑factors accelerate progression, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: HPV 16/18 infection (central cause)
HIV infection – reduces immune clearance of HPV
Smoking
Long‑term oral contraceptive use
Early sexual debut & multiple partners

sections.p: Early disease is often asymptomatic; when symptoms appear they reflect local invasion or bleeding.
b: Post‑coital or intermenstrual bleeding
Persistent watery or foul discharge
Pelvic pain in advanced disease
Back pain, flank pain from ureteric obstruction

sections.p: Tests are chosen to confirm cancer, stage disease, and identify treatable co‑morbidities.

t.b: Screens for precancerous changes; abnormal result triggers colposcopy
Detects lung metastases; normal result does not exclude distant spread
Identify obstruction‑related renal impairment; elevated creatinine prompts imaging or stenting
Detects co‑infection that influences prognosis and treatment choice

sections.p: Complications arise from local invasion, treatment side‑effects, or systemic spread.
b: Ureteric obstruction → hydronephrosis and renal failure
Fistula formation (vesicovaginal, rectovaginal)
Severe anemia from chronic bleeding
Metastatic disease to lung, bone, liver

sections.p: Treatment follows stage: early disease is curable with surgery or radiotherapy; advanced disease requires chemoradiation and palliative care.
b: Stage I: radical hysterectomy (removes uterus, parametria, upper vagina) – preferred when surgery feasible
Stage II‑III: concurrent cisplatin‑based chemoradiation – cisplatin radiosensitises tumour
Stage IV or non‑resectable: palliative radiotherapy, analgesia, and management of obstruction (stent or nephrostomy)
HIV‑positive: start antiretroviral therapy before cancer treatment to improve immunity

sections.p: Surveillance detects recurrence; primary prevention targets HPV infection.
b: Every 3–6 months for 2 years post‑treatment: pelvic exam, cytology, symptom review
HPV vaccination (bivalent or quadrivalent) before sexual debut reduces incidence
Screening with HPV test or VIA every 3–5 years in low‑resource settings

sections.p: Conditions that cause similar bleeding or discharge may be mistaken for cervical cancer.
b: Cervicitis (infectious)
Endometrial cancer (post‑menopausal bleeding)
Vaginal atrophy
Benign polyps

sections.p: Certain tests may give false reassurance.
b: Negative Pap smear in presence of high‑risk HPV can miss early invasive disease – proceed to colposcopy if symptoms persist
Normal renal function despite early ureteric obstruction – imaging needed if flank pain or rising creatinine

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden swelling of legs or abdomen

faq.q: Why is HPV the main cause of cervical cancer?
faq.a: High‑risk HPV integrates into cervical cells, producing oncoproteins that disable tumor suppressors, leading to uncontrolled growth.
Yes, through HPV vaccination and regular screening, which detect and treat precancerous lesions before they become invasive.

faq.q: What is the role of HIV in cervical cancer?
faq.a: HIV weakens immune surveillance, allowing persistent HPV infection and faster progression to cancer.

exam: Explain how FIGO staging guides treatment choices for cervical cancer.
Describe the screening algorithm for a 35‑year‑old woman in a low‑resource setting.
Discuss why concurrent cisplatin chemoradiation is the standard for locally advanced disease.
